articles.title: In 2011, Judy Garland's former Bel-Air home sold for $5.2 million; after successive renovations, the 1938 house on nearly 2.7 acres changed hands again for $11.1 million in July 2024
articles.summary: Judy Garland’s former Bel-Air home has changed hands for $11.1 million, more than a decade after it sold for $5.2 million.
articles.body: Judy Garland’s former Bel-Air home has changed hands for $11.1 million, more than a decade after it sold for $5.2 million. The 1938 estate at 1231 Stone Canyon Road was listed for $11.495 million in March 2024 before selling in July, according to property records and reports from The Real Deal, Realtor.com and Architectural Digest. The house carries a particularly strong connection to Garland’s early Hollywood years. She was 16 when the residence was commissioned, and 1938 was also the year she was cast as Dorothy Gale in The Wizard of Oz. Designed by celebrated architect Wallace Neff, the traditional-style home was created for Garland and her family and remains one of the properties associated with the actress’s rise to stardom.Set on roughly 2.66 acres, the estate combines the scale of an old Hollywood property with updates made by later owners. The 5,513-square-foot house has five bedrooms and seven bathrooms, with the grounds including a swimming pool and a separate writer’s cottage. The property is also located close to Sunset Boulevard and the Hotel Bel-Air, placing it within one of Los Angeles’ most established luxury residential areas.Its architectural character has remained an important part of the home’s appeal. The entrance opens into a grand foyer with a sweeping staircase and wrought-iron railing, while the interiors retain features such as hardwood flooring, storybook-style windows and traditional moulding. Later renovations introduced more contemporary luxury without completely removing the character of the original house.The kitchen was updated with modern appliances and a large marble island, while the adjoining breakfast area makes use of a bay window. The primary suite includes a fireplace, high ceilings, built-in storage and a dressing area. French doors and large windows help connect several of the living spaces with the surrounding grounds.Outside, the property has landscaped lawns, a brick-lined patio and a pool area. The detached cottage adds another layer to the estate and has been described as a writer’s studio. The combination of expansive grounds and a relatively intimate main residence gives the property the feel of a private Hollywood retreat rather than a newly built mega-mansion.Garland’s connection to the house goes beyond its construction date. Historical records identify 1231 Stone Canyon Road as the Judy Garland Residence, while accounts of her life place her there with members of her family during her teenage years. The house was part of the Stone Canyon Road area that attracted several entertainment-industry figures during Hollywood’s Golden Age.The property has also had a notable ownership history since Garland’s time. It sold for $5.2 million in February 2011, according to property records. It was then listed for $7.1 million in 2012 and sold for about $6.77 million that April. The home remained with the Chozen family until its 2024 sale.The 2024 transaction represented a substantial increase from the property’s 2011 sale price. After being placed on the market at nearly $11.5 million, the estate ultimately sold for $11.1 million, according to The Real Deal and the property’s sales record. The buyer’s identity was not publicly disclosed at the time of the sale.More than 85 years after Garland’s family first moved into the house, its biggest draw remains its connection to a defining chapter of Hollywood history. Unlike many celebrity properties that are heavily altered or replaced over the decades, the Stone Canyon residence continues to retain elements of its original architectural identity while accommodating the expectations of a modern luxury home.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Massive rush, traffic jams hit Himachal, Uttarakhand roads as tourists head to hills on long weekend
articles.summary: DEHRADUN: The three-day Gandhi Jayanti weekend has triggered a heavy rush of tourists and pilgrims in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, with traffic
articles.body: DEHRADUN: The three-day Gandhi Jayanti weekend has triggered a heavy rush of tourists and pilgrims in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, with traffic congestion reported on key routes leading to Manali, Shimla and Mussoorie, as well as pilgrimage sites including Badrinath, Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri.The rush followed the October 2 government holiday, with tourists using the extended weekend to travel to hill stations while pilgrims headed to Uttarakhand's Char Dham shrines.Heavy traffic on Chandigarh-Shimla routeThe Chandigarh-Shimla National Highway-5 witnessed heavy traffic on Friday as tourists headed towards Himachal Pradesh. Long queues of vehicles were reported on the Kalka-Shimla highway, with traffic moving slowly for several hours.The journey, which normally takes around three-and-a-half to four hours, was taking several additional hours amid the traffic surge. Vehicles were lined up for several kilometres, while traffic personnel were deployed at various points to regulate movement.The congestion also affected local residents and vehicles providing essential services.Manali sees heavy tourist rushA visuals shared by news agency ANI, Manali witnessed a major influx of tourists during the long weekend, leading to congestion on several mountain roads as long queues of vehicles as tourists arrived in large numbers.Seven-km jam on Badrinath routeIn Uttarakhand, heavy congestion was reported on the routes to Badrinath Dham and Hemkund Sahib as pilgrim numbers increased during the long weekend.A traffic jam stretching around seven kilometres was reported between Joshimath and Marwari, with vehicles queued from the Zero Band area towards Marwari. Pilgrims reportedly took between one and three hours to cover the stretch, with traffic moving briefly before coming to a halt again.The congestion also raised safety concerns as some vehicles were forced close to the edge of the road. The route had witnessed traffic problems during the monsoon as well, with congestion resurfacing during the final phase of the pilgrimage season.The Hemkund Sahib pilgrimage is also in its final phase, while the ongoing Pitru Paksha period has kept the flow of devotees to Badrinath Dham steady.Char Dham routes see increased pilgrim movementThe weekend rush also led to increased movement of pilgrims on other Char Dham routes.Rudraprayag Police shared post on X and said that the number of devotees visiting Kedarnath Dham had increased sharply due to the weekend, with pilgrims seen waiting in queues and moving towards the shuttle service.Meanwhile, Uttarkashi Police also posted on X and said the pilgrimage to Gangotri and Yamunotri Dham was proceeding smoothly, with the routes open and traffic moving without disruption.The heavy tourist and pilgrim movement across the two states has resulted in prolonged delays on several routes during the extended weekend.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news. articles.title: 55 Indians still in Russian army: New Delhi presses Moscow at key meet, take action against agents
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Around 140 Indian nationals recruited into the Russian army have been discharged, while India is seeking information on the whereabouts of 55
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Around 140 Indian nationals recruited into the Russian army have been discharged, while India is seeking information on the whereabouts of 55 others reportedly serving in the Russian armed forces, according to the details from India-Russia consultative committee meeting as cited by news agency ANI.New Delhi has engaged with Russian authorities for the early discharge of all such individuals."The government of India engaged with Russian authorities, including at the highest levels, for the early discharge of all such individuals. So far, around 140 Indian nationals have been discharged. Indian side is in touch with Russian authorities for the whereabouts of 55 Indian nationals who are reportedly in the Russian Army. Strong action being taken by the Indian law enforcement authorities against unscrupulous agents," the update from the meeting said.The latest figures are broadly in line with those shared by foreign secretary Vikram Misri last month. At the time, Misri said 139 of the 227 Indian nationals recruited into the Russian armed forces had been discharged, while 51 had died.Misri said the issue had been raised with Russia “at various levels on various occasions”.“At last count, we had information about 227 Indian nationals who had been recruited into the Russian army,” Misri had said. “Out of that, we have information that 139 of our nationals have been discharged from the army. And unfortunately, of course, we have information also about 51 people who have perished so far.”Misri had said India remained in constant discussions with Moscow to secure the early discharge and repatriation of those still serving.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: China’s Zijinshan gold mine turned its own waste into haul-road material; test roads carried 100-ton trucks and resisted deformation
articles.summary: A gold and copper mine in Longyan, China, has shown that its own waste can become the road beneath its heaviest vehicles.
articles.body: A gold and copper mine in Longyan, China, has shown that its own waste can become the road beneath its heaviest vehicles. According to ‘Sustainable valorisation of mine-derived solid wastes into cementitious pavement materials: Mechanical performance and microstructural insights,’ researchers mixed blasting slag, neutralised dreg and a binder made from steel slag, waste cement and lime slag, all taken from the Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine, then laid test roads that carried 100-ton trucks. After 28 days, the best mixture resisted deformation better than rock, soil and plain blasting slag, and it met groundwater limits for three toxic metals. This article explains how the mixture works, what the field tests found, and what limits remain, using a recent study.Why open-pit gold mines in China need stronger haul roads and a better use for stockpiled mine wasteOpen-pit mining generates large volumes of solid waste, including blasting slag, waste rock and treatment residues, which need extensive land for disposal and storage. The roads that carry ore are also under heavy strain, because they face intense rainfall, wind erosion and flooding while taking repeated heavy loads, which leads to potholes, rutting and uneven settling.Two of the waste streams are especially common. Blasting slag is produced when ore is excavated, while neutralised dreg is a powder left over from treating acid mine drainage. The dreg is the harder material to reuse. It can contain heavy metals, so reusing it without careful testing could create environmental and engineering risks.How researchers turned blasting slag, neutralised dreg and steel slag into cementitious pavement materialThe research team, made up of Jia-Ming Wen, Xiu-Zhu Su, Yuliang Guo and Xian-Lei Fu, built the mixture entirely from material found at the mine. The binder, called composite solid waste, combined water-quenched steel slag, waste cement and lime slag in a ratio of 17 to 2 to 1 by dry weight. An equal mix of blasting slag and neutralised dreg packed down the most densely, reaching a maximum dry density of 2.09 grams per cubic centimetre.The samples were cured for only three days, which was a deliberate choice. Haul roads must be put into service quickly to keep material moving, and the mine's construction-to-service window was limited to 72 hours. As the binder content rose from 3 to 15 per cent, compressive strength climbed from 0.98 to 4.92 megapascals, and mixtures above 9 per cent met the 3.0 megapascal reference for cement-stabilised road bases.Microscope and pore analysis explained why. The binder produced calcium silicate hydrate gel and ettringite crystals that coated the slag particles and filled the gaps between them, and total pore volume fell from 0.257 to 0.171 millilitres per gram.How the recycled pavement base performed under 100-ton trucks at the Zijinshan Gold-Copper MineThe trials took place on main haul roads at the 670-metre and 730-metre levels of the waste dump area, where the mixtures with 9 and 15 per cent binder were applied, and the roads carry 100-ton truck traffic and seasonal rain. Each pavement base was 30 centimetres thick, and each test section covered about 2,500 square metres.After 28 days of service, the team measured how much each surface bent under load, where a lower figure means stronger resistance to deformation. The mixture with 15 per cent binder cut deflection by 97.19 per cent compared with a compacted blasting slag base, 63.90 per cent compared with rock, and 73.02 per cent compared with soil. The plain blasting slag base was the only one that failed the design limit, which the authors interpreted as deterioration after 28 days.The 9 per cent mixture performed worse. Its deflection was nearly ten times higher than the 15 per cent mixture, so the authors concluded that 15 per cent was better suited to long-term use.Environmental safety, heavy metal leaching and carbon emission savings of mine waste roadsThe safety results matter as much as the strength results. Untreated neutralised dreg released cadmium, mercury and chromium above the groundwater Class IV standard, even after long immersion. In the 15 per cent road base, those metals leached at 0.007, 0.00003 and 0.02 milligrams per litre, all within the standard.The carbon comparison also favoured the waste-based mixture. Cradle-to-gate emissions were about 7.5 kilograms of carbon dioxide per square metre for the new materials, against 14.043 for cement-stabilised and 13.430 for fly ash-stabilised bases. That works out to roughly 55 per cent lower than cement and about 53 per cent lower than fly ash.Cost, limitations and what comes next for recycled mine waste pavementThe authors estimated material costs of 5.86 US dollars per square metre for the 9 per cent mixture and 6.99 for the 15 per cent mixture, compared with 6.92 for cement-stabilised and 6.81 for fly ash-stabilised bases. Plain blasting slag was the cheapest at 5.65, and the authors described the 9 per cent mixture as the most cost-balanced choice. That sits awkwardly beside their field finding that 15 per cent performed better, so the right choice depends on how long a road must last.The authors are open about the limits. The work covers early-age strength, a 28-day field trial and emissions only up to the factory gate, so long-term performance and maintenance savings still need to be confirmed through extended monitoring.You use AI every day. articles.title: From ‘tareekh pe tareekh’ to justice within 3 years: Amit Shah hails BNS, overhaul of criminal laws
articles.summary: Union home minister Amit Shah on Saturday said the full implementation of India’s new criminal laws would enable cases to be disposed of within three
articles.body: Union home minister Amit Shah on Saturday said the full implementation of India’s new criminal laws would enable cases to be disposed of within three years, from the filing of an FIR to the Supreme Court.“India’s judicial system was once known for its ‘tareekh pe tareekh’ taunts, but now, with the full implementation of the new criminal laws, justice will be delivered within three years, from the filing of an FIR to the Supreme Court,” he said.Shah was addressing the conference after inaugurating an exhibition on the new criminal laws at Dussehra Ground in Bhopal’s BHEL area.The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) came into effect on July 1, 2024. Shah said the laws incorporate science and technology into forensic investigations and include provisions concerning women’s safety, mob lynching, missing children and terrorism.He said the laws enacted under British rule were intended to preserve that rule, while the new laws were designed to protect the “honour, property, and body of Indian citizens”.“The fundamental principle of these laws is justice, not punishment. The provision of punishment is only to deter criminals from committing crimes. After the full implementation of these laws, our criminal justice system will be among the most modern in the world,” Shah said.Shah also said the government was working on a detailed plan to ensure drug abuse becomes non-existent in Madhya Pradesh after December 31, 2029.Turning to the cooperative sector, Shah attacked the Congress alleging that since Independence, poeple involved in agriculture, rural development, and cooperatives had been demanding a separate ministry, but the then-ruling party “prevented the establishment of such a ministry for 75 years”.“Prime Minister Narendra Modi has given a new direction to the cooperative sector by establishing a separate Ministry of Cooperation. Our cowherds will benefit the most from this. Middlemen take a large share of the profit when milk is sold in the open market, but there is no place for them in the cooperative model,” he said.At the event, the foundation stone was laid for a Rs 255-crore milk processing plant in Ujjain, with a capacity of three lakh litres per day. articles.title: A shopper paid just C$5 for a painting at a Canadian donation centre in 2020; experts identified it as a David Bowie original, and it sold for C$108,120 at auction the following year
articles.summary: In 2020, a shopper browsing a household goods donation centre in South River, Ontario, spotted a small painting tucked among discarded items and paid just
articles.body: In 2020, a shopper browsing a household goods donation centre in South River, Ontario, spotted a small painting tucked among discarded items and paid just C$5 for it. The buyer soon noticed a label on the reverse reading David Bowie and contacted auction house Cowley Abbott to investigate. After research and correspondence with a Bowie specialist in the UK, experts confirmed the work as an original from the musician's Dead Heads series, and in June 2021 it sold at auction for C$108,120, setting a new global record for a David Bowie artwork, according to a post on Cowleyabbott.ca. Read on to know more here:From a donation bin to a global auctionThe painting, titled D Head XLVI, was found in the most unexpected of places, a donation centre for household goods in Northern Ontario. The consignor was astonished to see the label bearing Bowie's name and realised that the signature on the reverse was that of the artist himself.What began as a casual purchase for just C$5 quickly became a story that captured the attention of collectors and media outlets around the world. Cowley Abbott performed due diligence before listing the work, including direct correspondence with a David Bowie specialist in the United Kingdom. Their research confirmed that the painting was indeed by Bowie and was part of a series that he completed in the 1990s. The authentication process was crucial given the rarity of Bowie’s paintings at auction and the need to establish provenance for a work found in such an unlikely setting, according to the report.Bowie as a painter and collectorDavid Robert Jones, known to the world as David Bowie, was far more than a music icon. He studied art and design as a young man, a background that nurtured a lifelong love of fine art. Bowie was also a passionate collector and painter, influenced by modernist trends of the twentieth century including the German expressionists, Francis Bacon and the London School of painters.His own paintings rarely appeared at auction, which made the discovery of D Head XLVI all the more significant. The work carries stylistic echoes of those influences, blending expressionist energy with the bold, figurative approach associated with Bowie's visual identity. For collectors, the chance to own an original Bowie painting is rare, and the South River find offered exactly that opportunity.The Dead Heads series explainedBetween 1995 and 1997, Bowie created a series of approximately 47 works on canvas that he titled Dead Heads, or D Head for short. Each title included a non-sequential Roman numeral, giving the series a distinctive numbering system. The sitters for these portraits ranged from band members and friends to acquaintances and even self-portraits, highlighting Bowie’s broad circle of collaborators and influences, according to Cowley Abbott’s post.Some of the paintings in the series are thought to be inspired by Bowie’s Ziggy Stardust period, when his visual persona was just as influential as his music. D Head XLVI depicts a subject with long hair and a prominent profile, painted in an energetic and enigmatic style. The label did not confirm the sitter’s identity, but the work remains a rare representation from a renowned artist whose visual output is often overshadowed by his musical legacy.A record-breaking auction outcomeThe painting was offered at Cowley Abbott’s Spring International Art Auction, which closed June 24, 2021, and caught the attention of collectors in Canada and beyond. The pre-sale estimate was C$9,000 to C$12,000, given the uncertainty of a piece with such an unusual provenance. But bidding quickly exceeded those expectations, with the final hammer price reaching C$108,120, nearly ten times the high end of the estimate, according to a report by Cbc.ca. That achievement set a new world auction record for a David Bowie work, eclipsing past sales of his paintings. The mystique was enhanced by the fact the artwork was discovered in a donation center and the story struck a chord with art collectors and fans of Bowie. The story had a far reach after being picked up by media outlets including The Globe and Mail and The Daily Mail.Why the discovery connected with peopleThe story of a C$5 purchase that became a six-figure sale strikes a chord because it combines luck, curiosity and the lasting power of celebrity. The shopper who found the painting wasn’t out looking to buy art but rather stumbled on a piece that was worth far more than expected. That element of surprise is part of what makes stories such as this so beguiling. For the art world, the sale also underscored the value of provenance and authentication. A label on the reverse of a canvas can be the key to unlocking a work's history, and in this case it led directly to confirmation that the painting was by one of the twentieth century's most iconic figures. The Cowley Abbott blog notes that Bowie's own work rarely appears at auction, making each new discovery a significant event for collectors.Bowie's visual legacy beyond musicDavid Bowie’s paintings reveal a deeply personal side of his creative mind, far beyond his famous music and film roles. His love of visual art directly influenced his iconic stage alter egos and album covers. In works like D Head XLVI, he brought the same raw intensity and unique visual voice to the canvas that defined his legendary sound. When D Head XLVI sold for a record C$108,120, it demonstrated that collectors value his art as an integral piece of his cultural legacy. Beyond the astonishing profit for the buyer, it’s a great reminder that extraordinary treasures can hide in plain sight.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Psychology says never feeling like you fit in may be less about you and more about the environments that shaped how you see yourself
articles.summary: Feeling like you do not belong can be difficult to explain.
articles.body: Feeling like you do not belong can be difficult to explain. You may be surrounded by friends, classmates or colleagues and still feel as if everyone else understands an unwritten social rule that you somehow missed. Over time, that feeling can change from a question about your surroundings into a question about yourself. Instead of thinking, “Maybe these are not my people,” you may start wondering, “What is wrong with me?” Psychology suggests that this shift can matter. Our sense of belonging is influenced not only by how others treat us, but also by how we interpret those experiences. Research on belonging uncertainty has found that when people are unsure whether they are accepted in a social environment, they can become more sensitive to social signals and may interpret ambiguous experiences through the lens of belonging.That does not mean every person who feels left out has an unhealthy mindset. Sometimes a group genuinely is not accepting. But repeated experiences can shape the way we understand ourselves long after we leave the environment where those experiences happened.The people around you can become a mirrorChildren learn about themselves partly through their interactions with other people. A child who is repeatedly praised for being curious may begin to see curiosity as part of who they are. Another child who is constantly told they are too sensitive or too quiet may eventually start believing those descriptions. Psychologists refer to this process through concepts such as reflected appraisals, where people's beliefs about how others see them can influence their own self-concept. The reactions of parents, teachers, classmates and friends can therefore become part of the psychological mirror through which a person understands themselves.Consider a quiet child in two different classrooms. In one, teachers give students time to think, and classmates appreciate thoughtful answers. In another, students who speak quickly and confidently receive most of the attention. The child has not changed, but the response from the environment has. Yet children do not always have the perspective to think, “This environment values a different personality style.” They may instead conclude, “I am bad at making friends,” or “Nobody likes people like me.” That conclusion can become powerful when it is repeated.When “I don't fit in” becomes an identityA difficult experience does not automatically become a permanent belief. But repeated experiences can make certain interpretations feel increasingly familiar. A teenager who is left out of a group might think, “They did not invite me.” Later, the thought may become, “People never choose me.” Years later, when a colleague forgets to invite them for lunch, the brain may immediately recognise the situation as confirmation. The event is real, but the meaning attached to it may come from much earlier experiences. Researchers Gregory Walton and Geoffrey Cohen studied what they called “belonging uncertainty”, or uncertainty about whether one is accepted in a particular social setting. Their work suggested that this uncertainty can affect how people interpret difficulties and ambiguous social experiences.This helps explain why someone who has repeatedly felt excluded may notice small social cues that another person would barely register. A delayed message can feel like rejection. A quiet group chat can seem like evidence that nobody wants you there. Someone looking distracted during a conversation can be interpreted as proof that they are bored with you. Sometimes those interpretations are correct. Sometimes they are not. The important point is that an old expectation can influence how a new situation is understood.The problem may sometimes be the room, not youIt is also important not to turn this idea into another reason to blame yourself. Not every experience of exclusion is caused by insecurity. Some environments genuinely make people feel unwelcome. Friend groups can be cliquish, workplaces can be hostile and families can dismiss certain personalities or opinions. Research on belonging has repeatedly highlighted the importance of the environment itself. Stanford researchers have found that interventions designed to strengthen people's sense of belonging work particularly well when the surrounding environment provides genuine opportunities for acceptance and connection. That means there are two possibilities that can exist together.You may have developed an expectation of rejection because of your past. And you may also be in a place that genuinely is not a good fit. A person who loves quiet conversations may struggle in a group built around constant socialising. Someone who values creativity may feel uncomfortable in an environment focused entirely on competition. Someone who needs emotional openness may feel disconnected from people who rarely discuss personal matters. None of this automatically means something is wrong with them. Sometimes the more accurate sentence is not, “I don't fit in.” It is, “I don't fit in here.” That small difference can change the entire meaning.Your past can shape you without defining youThe feeling of not belonging can follow people into adulthood. A new workplace, friendship group or relationship may trigger an old expectation even when the circumstances are different. Someone may constantly compare themselves with people who seem to connect more easily. They may notice the one person who did not respond to them while overlooking the two people who genuinely wanted to continue the conversation. This does not necessarily mean they are imagining rejection. Their brain may simply be paying greater attention to information that fits a familiar story. The good news is that familiar stories can be questioned.Instead of immediately thinking, “They do not like me,” a person can ask, “What actually happened?” or “Is there another explanation?” They can also ask whether the current situation resembles an earlier experience that shaped their expectations. This is not about forcing yourself to believe that everyone likes you. It is about separating an event from the conclusion you draw from it. You may discover that you need to work on a particular social habit. You may realise that a relationship is unhealthy. Or you may simply find that you are surrounded by people who are not compatible with you. All three are different conclusions.Perhaps the healthiest form of belonging is not being accepted everywhere. It is having enough relationships and environments where you do not feel compelled to constantly edit yourself to earn acceptance. You were never supposed to fit into every room. Some rooms will not suit you. Some people will misunderstand you. Some relationships will end. But one difficult environment should not become evidence that you are fundamentally difficult to love, understand or accept. Sometimes the problem was never that you did not belong anywhere. You simply spent too long believing that one room represented the whole world.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: A Kansas artist spent 30 years filling his 70-acre property with metal sculptures; nearly 600 giant totems were later preserved
articles.summary: A Kansas artist spent roughly three decades turning his 70-acre property in Mullinville into an outdoor gallery of metal sculptures. M.T.
articles.body: A Kansas artist spent roughly three decades turning his 70-acre property in Mullinville into an outdoor gallery of metal sculptures. M.T. Liggett filled the roadside landscape with hundreds of tall totems, whirligigs and smaller pieces made from discarded metal and objects from everyday life. Many carried sharp political or social messages, while others drew on people and experiences from his own life. After Liggett died in 2017, efforts began to preserve this unique collection. The result is an art environment that still stands along the Kansas highways and continues to attract curious visitors.How did M.T. Liggett fill his 70-acre property with metal sculpturesLiggett was born in Mullinville in 1930 and did not begin making art until later in life. According to KC Studio, he was in his late 50s when he created his first sculpture, a gargoyle made after one of his horses died from poisoning. He believed the sculpture could keep away dark forces, and that first experiment eventually led to decades of metalworking.For the next 30 years, Liggett worked with an arc welder and other basic tools, turning discarded materials into sculptures. KC Studio says he used farm implement parts, road signs and railway equipment, while Kansas Tourism reported tractor parts, farm machinery and other found metal as materials for the installations.The work gradually spread along the fences of his property beside US Highway 400 and Kansas Highway 54. The Kohler Foundation records the site as more than 70 acres and says it eventually contained as many as 600 large and small metal totems, alongside more than 500 smaller hearts and other artworks.The roadside gallery became part of MullinvilleLiggett did not create a conventional sculpture park with carefully separated exhibits. Instead, the pieces became part of the landscape. Some stood high above the fence line, while others moved in the prairie wind.Atlas Obscura describes hundreds of metal sculptures that squeak and turn in the Kansas wind, with some reaching more than 20 feet in height. The site included abstract figures, whirligigs and sculptures made by welding together objects that had previously served very different purposes.The display also became difficult for passing motorists to ignore. KMUW reported that, in 2001, The Wichita Eagle recorded as many as 100 vehicles a day pulling onto the shoulders of US 400 or US 54 to look at and photograph the artwork. The attention became enough of a concern that the Kansas Department of Transportation installed emergency parking only signs. By then, the unique roadside collection had become closely associated with Mullinville itself.What did the sculptures say about politics and everyday lifeA large part of Liggett’s work dealt with politics, public figures and institutions. The sculptures did not stick to one side of the political spectrum. The Kohler Foundation describes them as pieces aimed at politicians, officials, international figures and anyone else who attracted Liggett’s critical attention.His approach was deliberately personal and direct. KC Studio notes that his subjects included politicians, the justice system, social issues and current events. Some pieces also referred to Greek mythology, friends and former wives.Folkartwork describes the collection as deliberately broad in its targets instead of being devoted to a single political viewpoint. Its account notes that Liggett criticised figures from different political camps and used the sculptures to express strong opinions instead of showing a consistent party message.That mixture helped make the site both humorous and uncomfortable. Some of the sculptures worked almost like oversized political cartoons, using exaggerated forms and words to make their point. Atlas Obscura notes that Liggett also made pieces depicting his dogs, former wives and other subjects that were more personal than political.The collection was preserved after Liggett diedLiggett died on 17 August 2017, leaving behind a collection that was too large and unusual to treat as an ordinary group of artworks. SPACES Archives reports that his 70-acre property contained as many as 600 small and large metal totems, and that the Kohler Foundation became involved in preserving the site after being contacted by Liggett’s family and estate trustees.The preservation work began in April 2019, according to KMUW. The Kohler Foundation funded and directed the project, while the wider effort included conservation of the sculptures and construction of a visitor centre.Kohler Foundation says conservation treatment continued for two years and that the new visitor centre includes salvaged materials from Liggett’s original studio, along with some of his tools. The centre also provides a restoration area and workshop for maintaining the large totems and smaller artworks.The visitor centre keeps more than sculptures aliveThe preservation project was not limited to keeping the metal pieces standing. The visitor centre also helps tell the story behind them. KMUW reports that the building contains interactive videos featuring relatives, friends, Mullinville residents and people from the art world who knew Liggett or his work. His tools, clothing and collection of more than 6,000 coffee mugs are also displayed there.The original studio and shed, which Liggett called his Stew-Dee-Owe, was demolished in 2019 because of safety problems. Materials from that space were salvaged and incorporated into the preservation effort.The visitor centre also has an artist-in-residence programme, giving the site a role beyond simply displaying Liggett’s work. According to KMUW, the centre continues the preservation process while offering visitors a closer look at the artist and his methods.Liggett’s death did not end the public interest in his work. KMUW reported that more than 2,000 people stopped in Mullinville in the year before its 2023 report, while visitors came from 46 US states and 8 countries. The Kohler Foundation eventually gifted the preserved site to 5.4.7. Art Center of Greensburg in August 2021. Many members of the centre’s board had been friends of Liggett, according to the foundation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 5 Indian-origin men arrested in Canada over alleged extortion, shootings, arson & drug offences
articles.summary: Five Indian-origin men have been arrested and charged in Canada in connection with an alleged extortion campaign involving shootings, arson, firearms
articles.body: Five Indian-origin men have been arrested and charged in Canada in connection with an alleged extortion campaign involving shootings, arson, firearms trafficking and drug offences, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) reported.The arrests followed a 16-month investigation into an auto dealership whose co-owners reported receiving extortion demands in June 2025.The business was later targeted in two attacks involving arson and shootings at its locations in Langley and Surrey, the RCMP said in a statement on Friday.Police described the five accused as "foreign nationals", news agency PTI reported. One of the accused, 23-year-old Sanket Singla, is from India. He was arrested on Thursday at Toronto Pearson International Airport after investigators facilitated his entry into Canada, according to the RCMP.The other four accused, Sahil, 24, Simranjeet Singh, 24, Harsh, 21, and Jagdeep Singh, 24, were arrested in Surrey. Sahil, Simranjeet Singh and Harsh are residents of British Columbia, while Jagdeep Singh lives in Ontario. All five remain in custody, police said.The British Columbia Prosecution Service charged all five with extortion on Thursday. Some of the accused also face additional charges related to firearms, arson, explosives and cocaine trafficking.According to CBC News, Singla and Simranjeet Singh are accused of damaging a vehicle by fire or explosion and throwing Molotov cocktails into the auto shop with the intention of destroying or damaging property.Sahil also faces charges of cocaine trafficking and transferring prohibited firearms, the report said. The investigation resulted in the seizure of four firearms, ammunition and magazines, along with suspected fentanyl, cocaine and opium, the RCMP said.Police said evidence gathered during the investigation could be linked to other extortion and violence cases in British Columbia and Alberta. Further charges may follow, they added.The arrests are among a series of cases being investigated following the launch of a province-wide extortion task force last year, The Canadian Press reported. The cases have largely involved threats against business owners and members of the South Asian community, the report added.Chief Superintendent Duncan Pound of the BC extortion task force said it would emerge during court proceedings whether the Lawrence Bishnoi gang was involved in the cases.Pound also said alleged perpetrators in some investigations had claimed links to prominent gangs to increase intimidation, while noting that extortion was also a means of making money.The Canadian government designated the transnational criminal syndicate led by imprisoned Indian gangster Lawrence Bishnoi as a terrorist entity in September 2025. articles.body: Hazaribag: Hunterganj police in Chatra district have arrested a wanted criminal from Bihar’s list of top 10 offenders and recovered a stolen SUV from his possession, officers said on Saturday.The accused, Rambhajju Yadav alias Preman Yadav, 35, a resident of Rebda village in Bihar’s Gaya district, was arrested on Friday following a tip-off received by Chatra SP Animesh Naithany. articles.title: From pantry staple to pure Rajasthani comfort: Chef Ranveer Brar’s lightning-fast sev ki sabzi turns everyday kitchen leftovers into flavour-packed weeknight magic
articles.summary: There are evenings when the fridge looks emptier than you expected and the clock is already pushing dinner time.
articles.body: There are evenings when the fridge looks emptier than you expected and the clock is already pushing dinner time. No fresh vegetables staring back at you, just the usual pantry staples; a packet of crispy sev, some onions, tomatoes, curd and the everyday spices.In many Rajasthani and Malwa homes, that is exactly when sev ki sabzi comes to the rescue. Celebrity chef and MasterChef India judge Ranveer Brar has now put his own quick spin on this classic, showing how the same humble ingredients can turn into a flavour-packed sabzi in roughly ten minutes of active cooking.His recent YouTube video on his channel has brought the dish back into conversation, reminding people that comfort food does not always need long hours or fancy produce.Sev itself has deep roots in the dry regions of western and central India. The crisp gram-flour strands, especially the spicy Ratlami or Bhildi variety, grew out of practical needs in arid landscapes where fresh vegetables were not always easy to find.Over time, cooks began tossing the ready-made sev into a simple tomato or curd-based gravy, creating a dish that felt both filling and familiar. Brar’s version stays true to that spirit while keeping the process light and fast enough for a regular weeknight.A dish born from pantry wisdomSev ki sabzi belongs to that practical school of Indian cooking that thrives when the market run has not happened. In Rajasthan and neighbouring Malwa, people have long relied on shelf-stable ingredients like besan sev, dried spices and dairy to stretch a meal.The sev soaks up the gravy, softens just enough, and still keeps a pleasant bite. Brar highlighted this quality in his video, calling the dish ideal for days when you want something delicious without spending hours in the kitchen. He used a lightly spiced onion-tomato base enriched with beaten curd, which gives the gravy body and a gentle tang that balances the heat of the sev.The beauty lies in how little you need. A handful of pantry items; ghee, cumin, fennel, Kashmiri chillies, onions, ginger, green chillies, curd, one tomato and the sev itself, is enough. That simplicity is what has kept the dish alive across generations and why it still feels relevant today.How the ten-minute version comes togetherBrar’s method begins with a coarse ginger-green chilli paste and a thinned curd mixture that already carries a little ginger-garlic paste. In a hot kadai he tempered cumin seeds, fennel seeds, dried Kashmiri red chillies and a pinch of asafoetida in ghee.Roughly sliced onions go in next and cook until translucent. The ginger-chilli paste, degi chilli powder, turmeric, coriander powder and tender coriander stems follow quickly. A splash of water keeps the spices from burning while they release their aroma.The prepared curd mixture is poured in next and brought to a gentle simmer, stirred constantly so the curd does not split. Once it is bubbling, diced tomato, the masala sev, a little more water and a touch of sugar are added. Two or three minutes later the sev has softened into the gravy and the dish is ready.A final garnish of extra sev and a coriander sprig finishes it. What makes the dish linger in memory is the contrast of textures; soft, spicy gravy clinging to still-crisp bits of sev and the way the flavours hit all at once: heat, tang, a hint of sweetness and the nuttiness of gram flour.Brar suggested serving it hot with roti or bajra rotla, the way many families in Rajasthan still do. The same plate works just as well with plain rice when that is all you have.In a time when people often feel pressed for both time and ingredients, recipes like this one quietly prove that good food does not have to be complicated. Sev ki sabzi takes what is already sitting in the kitchen and turns it into something warm, satisfying and full of character. Ranveer Brar’s quick take simply makes that tradition easier to reach on an ordinary evening.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: 'You said it is AAP's initiative': Congress says CJP took 'instructions from Kejriwal' during Assam outreach
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress spokesperson Reetam Singh has claimed that Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka refused to meet Congress leaders
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress spokesperson Reetam Singh has claimed that Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka refused to meet Congress leaders during his recent Assam visit. He alleged that the group was told to stay away because its outreach was "an Aam Aadmi Party initiative".Singh's response came after Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das called out a fake "liberal ecosystem", saying that they believed they were alone responsible for “saving India, saving constitution”. However, they did not name Congress directly.Singh made the allegation in a post on X on Saturday while responding to Ranka, who had criticised what he described as an “entire ‘self-declared liberal’ ecosystem” targeting CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke.Singh said Congress workers had helped CJP members after they were detained by Assam Police and claimed that Ranka nevertheless declined a courtesy meeting with Congress leaders, including Assam Congress president Gaurav Gogoi.This comes days after Ranka and more than 40 CJP volunteers were detained in Guwahati ahead of a regional volunteers' meeting. Opposition parties, including Congress, AAP, the Assam Jatiya Parishad and Raijor Dal, had criticised the police action.'You asked us to stay out of it'Addressing Ranka, Singh said Congress members had helped secure the release of CJP workers after their detention.“When you were detained by Assam Police. We, Congress people helped to get CJP people out. Yet you categorically refused to have even a courtesy meeting with our Congress leaders and Gaurav Sir,” Singh said."You refused it because the Aam Aadmi Party asked you to not to. Kunki Chowdhury who was your Host in Guwahati, was on Election Campaign with AJP President Lurin Gogoi Da for a Congress Candidate in Nagaon. Even they had asked you to meet and discuss with Congress. Yet not once, you chose to engage with Congress or our students wing. You asked us to stay out of it. And that it is a Aam Aadmi Party initiative," he added.Singh also referred to Kunki Chowdhury, at whose residence Ranka and other CJP members were reportedly detained. He claimed Chowdhury had asked Ranka to meet Congress leaders and discuss the group's activities.CJP members had been detained from the residence of Assam Jatiya Parishad leader Kunki Chowdhury in the Dispur area ahead of their scheduled meeting.'Sidelined Neha Bora'Singh further accused Ranka and CJP of trying to portray the movement as an AAP initiative and referred to the group's earlier protests in Delhi.“We know how you sidelined Neha Bora in the Jantar Mantar 1.0 protests and when even Left chose to engage with our Leader Rahul Gandhi Ji. You decided you will not engage under direct instructions of Arvind Kejriwal,” he said.He also alleged that AAP had previously sought to associate itself with movements led by others, citing the India Against Corruption movement and activist Sonam Wangchuk's protest.“Aam Aadmi Party is known for piggy riding and hijacking issues of others,” Singh said.Singh said CJP was “a people's movement” and argued that it should not be treated as the property of any political party.“Let us keep it civil and issue centric. The cause is bigger than a political party,” he said.“CJP is a decentralised movement. There is no one Supreme Leader or his hierarchy. We all are equals. That is why people support it.”Row follows Ranka's criticismRanka's post that triggered Singh's response had accused a “self-declared liberal” group of targeting Dipke and questioning his growing reach.“An entire “self-declared liberal” ecosystem has been activated to denounce @abhijeet_dipke and the fact that he has been able to capture the imagination of millions of Indians after a LONG LONG time,” Ranka said.CJP co-convenor Saurav Das also criticised what he described as a group from outside the BJP that believed it alone was responsible for “saving India, saving constitution”. Neither Ranka nor Das named a political party in their posts."It’s a very big problem. A certain section—not just the BJP—another party thinks “saving India, saving constitution” is only their job. They are self-declared liberals and self-declared thekedars of the constitution," he said."It’s a very salty ecosystem, acting worse than the BJP’s ecosystem sometimes. They must realise that they can’t divide and rule through such tactics. Their massive failures over the years has led us to this moment where the young have to show the way. So they should just zip it on us and focus on how to support the young! Total buffoons!" he added.The latest exchange has brought CJP's political affiliations and its relationship with opposition parties into focus, even as the organisation continues its outreach on issues including education and electoral rolls.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
